questions.q: What is a "retry storm," as described in this lesson?
options: A cascading failure where simultaneous, immediate retries from many callers re-create the load that caused the original failure, preventing the struggling system from recovering
A single caller retrying one request too many times
A naturally occurring weather event that disrupts data centers
A retry strategy that always succeeds on the second attempt
questions.explain: A retry storm happens when many failed callers all retry immediately at once, adding to the load on an already-struggling system and preventing the recovery that reduced load might otherwise have allowed.

questions.q: What problem does exponential backoff solve, and what weakness does it still have on its own?
options: It eliminates the need for a maximum retry count, but introduces security risk
It solves jitter entirely and needs no further improvement

It waits progressively longer between attempts to give a struggling system breathing room, but callers that failed at the same moment will compute the same schedule and retry together again, still clustering
It only works for synchronous integrations, never asynchronous ones
questions.explain: Exponential backoff spaces out an individual caller's retries over increasing intervals, but without jitter, many callers that failed simultaneously will still retry in lockstep at each backoff step, re-creating a smaller-scale retry storm.

questions.q: What does jitter add to a retry strategy, and why is it usually paired with exponential backoff rather than used alone?
options: Jitter removes the need for any maximum retry count
Jitter adds randomized variation to each caller's wait time, spreading out retries that would otherwise cluster together — it solves a different half of the problem than backoff alone
Jitter guarantees the remote system will never fail again
Jitter is a synonym for exponential backoff with no functional difference
questions.explain: Jitter spreads retry timing across callers that failed simultaneously, which exponential backoff alone doesn't do — backoff and jitter solve two different halves of the retry-storm problem, which is why they're normally combined.

questions.q: What is a dead-letter queue, and what failure mode does it specifically avoid?
options: A queue that retries a failed message forever with no limit
A feature that automatically deletes failed messages without logging them
A queue used only for successfully processed messages, for audit purposes
A destination for a message that has exhausted its retry attempts, making the failure visible for human or process-level review instead of silently dropping it or retrying endlessly
questions.explain: A dead-letter queue is the deliberate middle ground between retrying forever and silently dropping a failed message — it surfaces the failure for review once retries are exhausted, directly avoiding the silent data loss failure mode from Lesson 2.

questions.q: Per this lesson, how do idempotency, backoff-with-jitter, and dead-letter handling relate to each other?
options: They form one coherent reliability design: idempotency makes a retry safe, backoff-with-jitter makes retrying responsible, and dead-letter handling makes an exhausted failure visible instead of silent
They are three unrelated, independent features that can each be adopted or skipped without affecting the others
Only one of the three is ever needed in a well-designed integration; the other two are redundant
Dead-letter handling replaces the need for idempotency entirely
questions.explain: Each piece covers a gap the others leave open — idempotency addresses whether retrying is safe, backoff-with-jitter addresses whether retrying is responsible toward the struggling system, and dead-letter handling addresses what happens once retries are exhausted.
